questions.ask: What exactly does this underlay-binding denote: a transport circuit itself, a binding/reference from an IP service to such a circuit, or a physical bearer? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Does this denote the physical client-facing demarcation where an underlay circuit meets client equipment, or a logical service attachment? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Is this the guaranteed end-to-end client payload rate, a physical bearer line rate, or another rate? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Does this denote measured one-way propagation delay of the transport circuit, or an IP-service latency objective/metric? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
Is this diverse-path transport protection against fiber/bearer failure, or service-level redundancy of another kind? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
What dimensions does this service class encode—for example transport protection/restoration, IP service tier, or something else? Please give a gloss, example, and relations.
What role does the VLAN encapsulation play, and to which concepts is it related? Please give a gloss and example.
What precisely is the IP service, and how does it relate to the underlay, attachments, VLAN, rate, latency, protection, and grade? Please give a gloss and example.

answers.gloss: The transport circuit itself, viewed from the IP-service model as the underlay to which a service is bound; it is not a separate binding object and not necessarily a physical bearer.
answers.example: IP service SVC-42 rides transport circuit U-7.
answers.relations: It carries c.service; conversely, c.service rides it. It is owned by the transport domain and referenced/consumed by the service domain.

answers.gloss: A logical customer-site attachment of an IP service, where that service meets the customer router; it is not inherently the physical circuit demarcation.
answers.example: att-NY-SVC42 is the New York attachment of SVC-42.
answers.relations: It is of c.service and bears c.vlan encapsulation.

answers.gloss: The committed information rate guaranteed to customer traffic by the IP service, not a physical bearer line rate.
answers.example: SVC-42 has a CIR of 5 Gbit/s.
answers.relations: It is an SLA/property of c.service.

answers.gloss: The IP service's latency commitment, represented as a named SLA tier rather than as a directly measured raw transport propagation delay.
answers.example: SVC-42 has latency tier T2, meaning no more than 8 ms.
answers.relations: It is an SLA/property of c.service; the commitment may depend operationally on the underlay but does not denote the underlay's measured delay.

answers.gloss: A service-level resilience requirement that the connectivity survive failure of its transport path.
answers.example: SVC-42 must remain connected after one underlay path failure.
answers.relations: It is a requirement/property of c.service and is realized through resilience in the transport underlay.

answers.gloss: The IP class of service applied to customer traffic, determining router scheduling and drop priority; it does not encode transport protection or restoration.
answers.example: SVC-42 uses the gold class and is assigned to a low-latency queue.
answers.relations: It is a traffic-treatment property of c.service.

answers.gloss: The customer VLAN tag used to identify the IP/Ethernet traffic at a particular logical service attachment.
answers.example: C-VLAN 100 identifies SVC-42 traffic at its New York attachment.
answers.relations: It is carried on c.attachment; the attachment belongs to c.service. It is not a physical transport bearer.

answers.gloss: The end-to-end IP/VPN service delivered to the customer. It rides a transport circuit that the transport domain knows only as a circuit, not as this IP service.
answers.example: SVC-42 is a point-to-point IP service connecting New York and Frankfurt.
answers.relations: It rides c.underlay and attaches at one or more c.attachment points, whose traffic may be identified by c.vlan. c.rate, c.latency, c.protection, and c.grade are service commitments or properties.

questions.ask: Does this denote the transport circuit itself, and can an IP/customer service ride or reference it? Please give its gloss, example, and relations, including how it differs from m.bearer.
Is this a physical/client-facing demarcation of a transport circuit, a logical service attachment, or both? Please give its gloss, example, and relations.
Does this denote bearer line rate, transport-circuit payload capacity/committed rate, or an end-to-end customer service CIR? Please give its gloss, example, and relations.
Is this a measured/raw transport-circuit delay or a named customer-service SLA commitment? Please give its gloss, example, and relations.
Does this denote implemented transport-path diversity/protection, a requested resilience objective, or both? Please give its gloss, example, and relations.
Which dimensions does transport grade encode, and does it include router scheduling/drop priority or instead transport engineering characteristics? Please give its gloss, example, and relations.
What entity does the bearer denote, how does it relate to m.circuit, and is it physical infrastructure, an encapsulation, or something else? Please give its gloss, example, and relations.

proposals.rationale: My underlay denotes the transport circuit itself as viewed and referenced by the IP-service domain, while A's catalogue identifies m.circuit as a transport circuit. Confirmation depends on A's detailed distinction between circuit and bearer.

answers.gloss: The provisioned transport circuit carrying a client end to end across the optical core. An external IP/customer service can ride or reference it as its underlay. Unlike m.bearer, it is the end-to-end client-facing transport construct rather than the internal optical wavelength carrying it.
answers.example: CIR-7 runs from the New York hand-off to the Frankfurt hand-off and may underlie IP service SVC-42.
answers.relations: It presents at m.handoff and is carried on m.bearer. It can serve as the transport underlay for an external service, although that service is not represented in my model.

answers.gloss: The physical client-facing demarcation where a transport circuit presents to customer equipment; it is not the logical attachment of an IP service.
answers.example: The New York hand-off port where CIR-7 meets the customer router.
answers.relations: It is on m.circuit. A logical service attachment could be configured at or over this location, but that attachment is a distinct concept absent from my model.

answers.gloss: The committed client payload rate guaranteed end to end by the transport circuit, not the optical bearer's line rate and not, in this model, an SLA property of a separately modeled IP service.
answers.example: CIR-7 guarantees 5 Gbit/s of committed payload capacity.
answers.relations: It is a property of m.circuit. It may constrain or support a service CIR, but it denotes the circuit's commitment rather than the service-domain property.

answers.gloss: The measured one-way propagation delay of the transport circuit, expressed as a raw duration determined by its path length; it is not a named customer-service SLA tier.
answers.example: CIR-7's primary path has a measured one-way latency of 7.2 ms.
answers.relations: It is a property of m.circuit. A service latency commitment may depend on it, but is not identical to it.

answers.gloss: Implemented transport-path protection of a circuit, switching traffic to a diverse path after fiber-cut or bearer failure; it is not merely a service-level resilience request.
answers.example: CIR-7 uses 1+1 path protection so a cut on its primary fiber triggers use of the diverse path.
answers.relations: It is a property/configuration of m.circuit and is realized within the transport network. It can satisfy an external service resilience requirement, but the requirement and implementation are distinct.

answers.gloss: The circuit's transport quality grade, encoding physical protection and restoration class. It does not denote router queue scheduling, traffic priority, or drop behavior.
answers.example: CIR-7 is platinum grade because it has dual-path transport protection; other grades include gold and best-effort.
answers.relations: It is a property of m.circuit and summarizes transport engineering characteristics such as protection/restoration.

answers.gloss: A physical optical bearer—specifically a wavelength or lambda on fiber—on which transport circuits are carried. It is internal physical transport infrastructure, not a VLAN or other service encapsulation.
answers.example: The 193.1 THz wavelength on the New York–Frankfurt span carries CIR-7.
answers.relations: It carries m.circuit; one bearer may support circuit transport, while the circuit is the end-to-end construct presented through m.handoff.

ratifications.reason: Both denote the transport circuit itself. c.underlay names that same circuit from the consuming IP-service perspective, whereas m.circuit models it in the transport domain. Neither denotes the lower-level optical bearer.
